term:NIST AI RMF Playbook.deep_dive: The AI RMF's companion how-to: for every subcategory of the four functions, suggested actions, informative references, and documentation guidance — turning the framework's what into implementable how. Online, evolving, and explicitly non-mandatory: organizations pick actions proportionate to their context.
term:NIST AI RMF Playbook.exam_tip: Framework = the RMF itself; Playbook = the per-subcategory action guide — the pairing question is common.

term:NIST AI Risk Management Framework (.deep_dive: The US voluntary framework (1.0, January 2023) for trustworthy AI: risk framing plus seven trustworthiness characteristics plus the four-function Core — Govern (cross-cutting), Map (context), Measure (assessment), Manage (response). Sector-agnostic, rights-preserving, and the de facto US governance vocabulary.
term:NIST AI Risk Management Framework (.exam_tip: Four functions and seven characteristics — the two lists to know cold; Govern surrounds, not precedes, the others.

term:Named Entity Recognition (NER).deep_dive: The NLP task of finding and classifying named entities — people, organizations, locations, dates — in text. Governance relevance: NER is how pipelines detect personal data at scale, making it both a privacy-compliance tool (PII discovery) and a privacy risk (systematic identification).
term:Named Entity Recognition (NER).exam_tip: ISO 22989 task vocabulary — recognize it as the PII-detection workhorse in data governance tooling.

term:National Competent Authorities (EU.deep_dive: Each member state's designated enforcers: at least one notifying authority (accrediting conformity-assessment bodies) and one market surveillance authority (investigating, correcting, penalizing) — due for designation by August 2025, coordinating through the European AI Board.
term:National Competent Authorities (EU.exam_tip: National authorities handle AI systems; the EU-level AI Office handles GPAI — the two-tier enforcement split recurs.

term:Natural Language.deep_dive: Human language as humans actually produce it — ambiguous, contextual, evolving — as distinct from formal languages built for machines. Its messiness is why NLP is hard and why language-model errors are subtle: fluent form conceals unreliable content.
term:Natural Language.exam_tip: Contrast anchor: natural language (human, ambiguous) vs. programming language (formal, exact) — a definitional distractor pattern.

term:Natural Language Generation (NLG).deep_dive: The production side of language AI: generating human-readable text from data, structured inputs, or learned distributions — from template-driven report writing to free-form LLM generation. Its governance shadow is confabulation: fluency without guaranteed truth.
term:Natural Language Generation (NLG).exam_tip: NLU understands input; NLG produces output — the U/G split inside NLP is tested at recognition level.

term:Natural Language Understanding (NLU.deep_dive: The comprehension side of NLP: extracting meaning, intent, and structure from human language — intent classification, entity extraction, semantic parsing. It's what lets a system act on 'cancel my subscription' — and misunderstanding at this layer propagates into wrong actions downstream.
term:Natural Language Understanding (NLU.exam_tip: Understanding (NLU) in, generation (NLG) out — match the definition to the direction.

term:Neuron.deep_dive: The network's atomic unit: receives weighted inputs, sums them, applies an activation function, passes the signal on. Individually trivial, collectively capable — intelligence emerges from scale and connection, which is the connectionist thesis in one component.
term:Neuron.exam_tip: Anatomy vocabulary: neuron (unit) → layer (collection) → network (architecture); weights are learned, activations are chosen.

term:Non-Discrimination Law.deep_dive: The legal regime prohibiting discrimination on protected characteristics — reaching AI through disparate treatment (intentional) and disparate impact (effect-based) doctrines under Title VII, ECOA, FHA, ADA, ADEA, and EU equality law. Algorithms discriminate at scale and through proxies, which is exactly the pattern impact doctrine was built to catch.
term:Non-Discrimination Law.exam_tip: Facially neutral + disproportionate harm + weak business justification = disparate impact — the algorithmic fact pattern to recognize.

term:Notice.deep_dive: The transparency obligation: telling individuals what data is collected, why, on what basis, shared with whom, kept how long, and what rights they hold — before or at collection (GDPR Arts 13-14). AI strains notice because future model uses resist description at collection time — which doesn't excuse the obligation.
term:Notice.exam_tip: Notice informs, consent authorizes — they're distinct duties; buried or vague AI-training notice is a recurring violation pattern.

term:OECD AI Principles.deep_dive: The 2019 intergovernmental consensus (updated 2024): five values — inclusive growth and well-being; human rights and democratic values including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability — plus five policy recommendations. The vocabulary source for 'trustworthy AI' worldwide and the definitional anchor the EU AI Act aligned to.
term:OECD AI Principles.exam_tip: Five values + five recommendations; first intergovernmental AI standard; the AI-system definition other instruments borrow.

term:Open Source Agreement.deep_dive: The license terms governing open-source models, code, and datasets — 'open' never means unconditioned: attribution, copyleft, use restrictions (some AI licenses bar specific applications), and no-warranty clauses all bind. AI supply chains stack licenses (base model + fine-tune data + libraries), and violations are IP violations.
term:Open Source Agreement.exam_tip: Open-source ≠ free-for-anything — license compliance review belongs in AI due diligence like any other rights check.

term:Operation & Monitoring.deep_dive: The ISO 22989 lifecycle stage where the system earns its keep under watch: serving predictions while telemetry tracks performance, drift, fairness, and security — the longest stage of the lifecycle and the one where reality diverges from validation assumptions.
term:Operation & Monitoring.exam_tip: Lifecycle-stage vocabulary: deployment puts it in production; operation & monitoring keeps it honest there.

term:Operational Controls.deep_dive: The running-state safeguards: access management on models and data, change management for updates, logging and audit trails, monitoring thresholds, incident procedures, and backup/recovery — the ISO 42001 Annex A territory that keeps a governed system governed day to day.
term:Operational Controls.exam_tip: Design controls prevent; operational controls sustain — scenarios about production hygiene (access, change, logs) point here.

term:Overfitting.deep_dive: The model that memorized instead of learned: capturing training-set noise and idiosyncrasy, acing training metrics, failing new data. Counters: more/better data, regularization, early stopping, simpler models — and honest validation on held-out data, which is how it's caught.
term:Overfitting.exam_tip: High training accuracy + poor real-world performance = overfitting; poor everywhere = underfitting — the signature pattern pair.

term:PDCA Cycle.deep_dive: Plan-Do-Check-Act: the continuous-improvement loop underneath every ISO management system — plan the AIMS, run it, audit and measure it, correct and improve it, repeat. It's why certification is a cycle of surveillance audits, not a one-time trophy.
term:PDCA Cycle.exam_tip: PDCA = the improvement engine inside ISO 42001; management systems iterate by design.

term:Parameter (Model Parameter).deep_dive: What training learns: the weights and biases encoding a model's knowledge — billions of them in modern LLMs. Contrast hyperparameters (set by humans before training). Parameter counts drive capability, cost — and regulatory attention, since compute thresholds proxy for parameter-scale capability.
term:Parameter (Model Parameter).exam_tip: Parameters learned, hyperparameters configured — and 'the model IS its parameters' explains why model theft and deletion questions target the weights.

term:Patent.deep_dive: The exclusive right for inventions — novel, non-obvious, useful. AI angles: algorithms and models can be patentable subject matter (within abstract-idea limits), but inventorship must be human — AI-generated inventions without a human inventor are unpatentable under current US/EU doctrine (the DABUS line).
term:Patent.exam_tip: Human inventor required — parallel to copyright's human-author rule; the symmetry makes both memorable.

term:Performance.deep_dive: How well a system does its job, measured against defined criteria — accuracy family, latency, throughput, robustness — with metric *choice* being the governance act: optimizing precision vs. recall encodes whose errors matter. Performance also decays: drift makes yesterday's metrics fiction.
term:Performance.exam_tip: Performance is multi-dimensional and metric choice is value-laden — 'high accuracy' alone never closes a governance question.

term:Personal Data (PbD).deep_dive: GDPR's expansive trigger: any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person — names, IDs, location, online identifiers, and combinations that single someone out. Includes inferences and pseudonymized data; excludes only the truly anonymous. If personal data is processed, the whole regime applies.
term:Personal Data (PbD).exam_tip: Identifiability is the test — indirect identification counts, inferences count, pseudonymized counts; the scope is deliberately wide.

term:Personally Identifiable Information.deep_dive: The US-flavored cousin of personal data: information that can identify a specific individual, alone or combined — the operative concept in US breach laws and federal privacy guidance. Narrower in spirit than GDPR's 'personal data,' which sweeps in relatability, not just identifiability.
term:Personally Identifiable Information.exam_tip: PII (US usage) ⊂ personal data (GDPR usage) roughly — cross-jurisdiction questions trade on the width difference.

term:Planning.deep_dive: Double duty: the classical-AI capability of computing action sequences toward goals, and the lifecycle/management activity (ISO 42001 clause 6) of setting objectives, assessing risks, and designing the roadmap before building. Exam context usually means the latter — governance starts at planning.
term:Planning.exam_tip: Read context: 'planning' in a lifecycle question = the pre-build governance stage; in an AI-capability list = classical action planning.

term:Post-Market Monitoring.deep_dive: The EU AI Act's mandated afterlife-watch: high-risk providers must run documented systems collecting and analyzing performance data from deployed systems, feeding corrective action and serious-incident reporting. Borrowed from medical-device law — approval is conditional on continued good behavior.
term:Post-Market Monitoring.exam_tip: Provider duty, mandatory for high-risk, documented plan required — 'we monitor informally' fails the standard.

term:Precision.deep_dive: Of everything the model flagged positive, the fraction actually positive — the metric that punishes false alarms. Traded against recall (catching everything real): fraud teams drowning in false positives need precision; cancer screening that must miss nothing needs recall.
term:Precision.exam_tip: Precision = trustworthy positives; recall = complete positives — pick per the cost of each error type in the scenario.

term:Predictability.deep_dive: ISO 22989 trustworthiness property: stakeholders can reliably anticipate how the system behaves — consistent outputs for similar inputs, stable behavior across versions, no surprises. Predictability underwrites trust calibration and oversight: humans can only supervise what they can anticipate.
term:Predictability.exam_tip: Trustworthiness-vocabulary item: predictability enables oversight — erratic systems defeat even well-designed human review.

term:Prediction.deep_dive: The basic act of inference: a model's estimate about something unknown — a class, a value, a next token, a risk score. Legally weightless until acted on: prediction becomes decision when it produces effects, which is where Article 22 and oversight duties attach.
term:Prediction.exam_tip: Prediction vs. decision: governance obligations concentrate where predictions drive effects on people.

term:Privacy.deep_dive: The individual's interest in controlling information about themselves and being free from unwarranted intrusion — the value data protection law operationalizes. AI pressures it uniquely: inference reveals the uncollected, aggregation defeats context, and models remember what databases forget.
term:Privacy.exam_tip: Privacy is the value; data protection is the legal machinery — and AI's inference power is the novel threat vector to name.

term:Privacy by Design.deep_dive: Building privacy into systems from conception — proactive not reactive, default-protective, embedded in architecture — codified in GDPR Article 25 (data protection by design and by default). For AI: minimization in pipelines, PETs in training, retention limits in models, and privacy review at design gates.
term:Privacy by Design.exam_tip: Article 25 makes it law, not aspiration — and 'by default' means the protective setting ships enabled.

term:Privacy-Enhanced.deep_dive: The NIST trustworthiness characteristic: the system incorporates norms and techniques safeguarding autonomy and identity — minimization, PETs, de-identification — by design. NIST's framing makes privacy a property of trustworthy AI, not a compliance afterthought.
term:Privacy-Enhanced.exam_tip: One of the seven NIST characteristics — recognize the list membership.

term:Probability Severity Matrix.deep_dive: The classic risk-visualization grid: likelihood on one axis, impact on the other, risks plotted into green/amber/red zones driving treatment priority. Simple, communicable, and honest about its ceiling — qualitative scoring invites false precision and gaming.
term:Probability Severity Matrix.exam_tip: Standard risk-prioritization tool: position = likelihood × severity; the red corner gets treated first.

term:Product Liability.deep_dive: Liability for harm caused by defective products — strict (no fault required) across manufacturing defects, design defects, and failure to warn. The EU's revised Product Liability Directive drags software and AI explicitly into scope, including harm from updates and learned behavior post-sale.
term:Product Liability.exam_tip: Strict liability = injury + defect suffices; the EU revision explicitly covering AI/software is the current-events fact.

term:Production Data.deep_dive: The live data a deployed system processes — real users, real stakes, real legal obligations, unlike curated training corpora. Two disciplines attach: monitoring it for drift from training assumptions, and governing any reuse of it for retraining (fresh purpose, fresh rights analysis).
term:Production Data.exam_tip: Using production data to retrain is a new processing purpose — the rights/compatibility analysis re-runs; it's not automatically permitted.

term:Production Readiness Evaluation.deep_dive: The pre-launch verdict across every readiness axis: documentation complete, conformity obligations met, stress and adversarial testing passed, monitoring wired, rollback planned, approvals signed. Its output is a governed go/no-go decision with named owners — the audit trail proving deployment was a choice, not a drift.
term:Production Readiness Evaluation.exam_tip: Readiness is technical AND governance — a scenario passing performance tests but missing signoffs or rollback plans is not ready.

term:Prohibited AI.deep_dive: The AI Act's banned list (Article 5, effective February 2025): social scoring by public authorities, exploitation of vulnerabilities causing harm, subliminal manipulation, untargeted facial-image scraping, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, biometric categorization inferring protected traits, and real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces — with narrow, warrant-like law-enforcement exceptions.
term:Prohibited AI.exam_tip: Memorize the list — 'spot the prohibited practice' is a near-guaranteed question, and the law-enforcement carve-outs are the nuance layer.

term:Pseudonymization.deep_dive: Replacing identifiers with pseudonyms while a re-linking key exists somewhere — GDPR names it as a security measure, and pseudonymized data remains fully personal data. Useful risk reduction, routinely mistaken for anonymization, which requires irreversibility.
term:Pseudonymization.exam_tip: Pseudonymized = still personal data, GDPR applies; anonymized = out of scope — the single most-tested privacy distinction.

term:Public Disclosure.deep_dive: Making information about AI systems public — transparency reports, incident announcements, registry entries (the EU database for high-risk systems), and legally compelled notices. Timing and accuracy are governed: premature disclosure can mislead, late disclosure compounds harm, false disclosure is its own violation.
term:Public Disclosure.exam_tip: Some disclosure is mandatory (EU database registration, breach notices), some strategic (transparency reports) — sort by obligation first.

term:Purpose Limitation.deep_dive: Data collected for specified purposes may not be processed incompatibly with them — the GDPR principle AI most reliably strains, since training is rarely the collection purpose. The path forward: compatibility analysis, or a fresh lawful basis with fresh transparency — never silent repurposing.
term:Purpose Limitation.exam_tip: 'We had the data anyway, so we trained on it' is the violation pattern — repurposing demands analysis or a new basis.

term:Quality Management System (QMS).deep_dive: The documented organizational machine ensuring consistent quality — processes, roles, records, improvement loops (ISO 9001 lineage). The AI Act requires high-risk providers to run one covering design, development, testing, and post-market phases; ISO 42001's AIMS deliberately docks with it.
term:Quality Management System (QMS).exam_tip: QMS is an explicit EU AI Act high-risk provider requirement — not just an ISO nicety.

term:Question Answering.deep_dive: The NLP task of answering natural-language questions — extractive (find the answer in text) or generative (compose it). Modern QA rides LLMs and RAG, inheriting confabulation risk: fluent answers with fabricated content, dangerous exactly in proportion to user trust.
term:Question Answering.exam_tip: ISO 22989 task vocabulary — with hallucination as the attached governance risk in generative form.

term:Reassessment.deep_dive: The scheduled or triggered re-run of governance evaluations — risk assessments, impact assessments, validations — because their conclusions age: models drift, contexts shift, regulations land, incidents teach. ISO 22989's lifecycle includes re-evaluation as a formal stage; mature programs predefine reassessment triggers.
term:Reassessment.exam_tip: Assessments are living documents — material change (system, data, context, law) reopens them; annual-at-minimum is the default pattern.

term:Recall.deep_dive: Of everything actually positive, the fraction the model caught — the metric that punishes misses. The precision trade-off is governance in miniature: screening for cancer maximizes recall (miss nothing), spam filtering leans precision (flag carefully).
term:Recall.exam_tip: Recall = completeness of catch; the cost of a miss vs. the cost of a false alarm decides which metric leads.

term:Record Keeping.deep_dive: The evidentiary discipline: contemporaneous, retrievable records of decisions, tests, approvals, incidents, and system events — with the AI Act adding automatic logging requirements for high-risk systems and 10-year documentation retention for providers. Records are how governance survives contact with auditors, regulators, and courts.
term:Record Keeping.exam_tip: High-risk systems must log automatically; providers keep technical documentation 10 years — the two AI Act record numbers.

term:Red Teaming.deep_dive: Structured adversarial exercise: dedicated attackers probing a system for failures before real adversaries and users find them — jailbreaks, injections, bias elicitation, unsafe outputs. Now institutionalized: NIST ARIA's middle evaluation level, an EU AI Act expectation for systemic-risk GPAI, and a pre-release readiness staple.
term:Red Teaming.exam_tip: Red teaming = offensive testing by design — required territory for systemic-risk GPAI and the canonical pre-deployment adversarial control.

term:Reliability.deep_dive: ISO-flavored trustworthiness: the system performs its intended function consistently under stated conditions — the steady-state cousin of robustness (which covers adverse and unexpected conditions). Reliability failures are availability and correctness failures users experience directly.
term:Reliability.exam_tip: Reliability = consistent intended behavior (normal conditions); robustness = holds up under stress (abnormal conditions) — ISO splits them.

term:Resilience.deep_dive: The bounce-back property: withstand disruption, degrade gracefully, recover fast — spanning infrastructure failover, model fallbacks, and attack recovery. NIST bundles it with security ('secure and resilient'): a trustworthy system survives both adversaries and accidents.
term:Resilience.exam_tip: Resilience is about recovery and graceful degradation — distinct from robustness (resisting failure in the first place).

term:Responsible AI.deep_dive: The umbrella practice of developing and deploying AI ethically, legally, and safely — the principle set (fairness, accountability, transparency, human-centricity, robustness, privacy) plus the organizational machinery that enforces it. Effectively synonymous with 'trustworthy AI' (NIST) and 'ethical AI' in most usage.
term:Responsible AI.exam_tip: Treat responsible/trustworthy/ethical AI as one concept family — the principles underneath are what get tested.

term:Retraining.deep_dive: Updating a model with new data to counter drift, add capability, or fix defects — a governed event, not a background process: retraining triggers defined in advance, new versions validated like new models, regression-tested against prior behavior, and documented for the audit trail.
term:Retraining.exam_tip: Monitoring detects degradation → investigate root cause → retrain if indicated → validate before release — retraining without diagnosis or validation is the planted error.

term:Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG.deep_dive: Grounding generation in retrieval: the system fetches relevant documents from a knowledge store and conditions the LLM's answer on them — reducing (not eliminating) confabulation, enabling citations, and keeping knowledge current without retraining. New risk surface: retrieved content can carry indirect prompt injections.
term:Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG.exam_tip: RAG = the standard hallucination mitigation — grounding in retrieved sources; but retrieval opens the indirect-injection door.

term:Right to Erasure.deep_dive: GDPR Article 17's 'right to be forgotten': individuals can demand deletion when data is no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, or processing was unlawful — with exceptions (legal obligations, public interest, claims). The AI frontier: what erasure means for models trained on the data, where retraining and machine unlearning are the live options.
term:Right to Erasure.exam_tip: Not absolute (exceptions exist) — and the model-trained-on-deleted-data question is the AI-specific twist to expect.

term:Risk.deep_dive: The governing abstraction: effect of uncertainty on objectives, operationalized as likelihood × severity of harm. Every framework tiers by it — the AI Act's ladder, the RMF's mapping, ISO's registers — because governance resources are finite and risk is how they're rationed.
term:Risk.exam_tip: Risk = likelihood × impact; inherent (before controls) vs. residual (after) — the vocabulary every scenario assumes.

term:Robustness.deep_dive: Holding up under the unexpected: maintaining performance on edge cases, distribution shifts, noisy inputs, and adversarial pressure — tested through stress testing, edge-case suites, and adversarial evaluation. OECD and NIST both enshrine it; brittleness is its failure mode.
term:Robustness.exam_tip: Robustness = performance under adverse/unusual conditions; reliability = consistency under normal ones — the tested pair.
